newsitem.title: USA: Miami used bond proceeds to hide deficit - official.
newsitem.headline: Miami used bond proceeds to hide deficit - official.

text.p: Miami temporarily parked $22 million of bond proceeds in its general fund account at the end of fiscal 1995 to conceal that it had a deficit for the year, assistant city manager Bill Hampton said on Thursday.

The money was raised in the August 18, 1995 sale of $22 million of special obligation non-ad valorem bonds, an issue sold to finance the purchase of an office building formerly owned by Florida Power & Light Co.

"The last day of the fiscal year, they parked it in the general fund. When you looked at the books at the end of the fiscal 1995, it looked like there was a surplus," Hampton told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"On October 4, they pulled the bond money out to buy this building," he said, referring to the city office building.

Several city officials have said that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Miami bond deals, but neither they nor the SEC would say whether or not the probe focuses on the use of bond proceeds.

Whether or not the temporary transfer of bond money into the general fund was legal, Hampton said, "it's a misrepresentation of the solvency" of the general fund and "a total violation of the cardinal principles of good government and good business."

The city's former outside auditors, Deloitte & Touche, did warn the city that it had a $26 million deficit for fiscal 1995, which ended September 30, 1995. It was unclear if they had noted the transfer of bond money into the general fund and officials with the firm were not immediately available for comment on Thursday.
Hampton said other bond proceeds had also been transferred into the general fund and some had been spent for purposes other than those specified in the bond documents.

"They used revenue bond funds to balance off deficits in the general fund. Now the general fund owes those bond projects about $20 million. If all of the projects listed for capital improvements became due and payable today, there would be $20 million in funding that couldn't be done," Hampton said. He said it was difficult to determine which money came from which issue.
"Because they pooled the cash, it's hard to say which ones are which," he said.

In addition to the bond issue for the office purchase, Miami issued $22.5 million of sewer system tax GO bonds in June of 1995 and $72 million of non-ad-valorem revenue bonds for unmet pension obligations in December of 1995.

Union pension boards previously raised questions about the proceeds from the pension bond issue, prompting a review. In a September 19,1996 memo, Acting City Manager Merrett Stierheim said the money had been tracked down and "there appears to be nothing irregular about the use of these bond monies."
The bond documents for that issue specifically said that some of the bond proceeds would be used to reimburse the city's general fund for that year's pension contribution.
Hampton, a court administrator with 40 years experience in government finance and administration, is among the corporate and government volunteers helping Stierheim draft a bail-out plan.
